title: Deep SiMLR: Auditable Multi-Modal Integration for Biomedical Discovery
text:
Abstract
Multi-modal biomedical datasets—such as co-registered neuroimaging, high-throughput omics, and clinical assessments—provide complementary views of shared pathological processes. Integrating these heterogeneous matrices requires dimensionality reduction that isolates cross-view covariance while maintaining interpretable feature attribution. Standard deep multi-view networks and variational autoencoders capture non-linear interactions, but their nested compositions obscure the physical relationship between raw biological measurements and latent coordinates, imposing a severe “transparency penalty” that precludes regulatory adoption in high-stakes clinical decision-making. Conversely, classical linear methods like Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) provide auditable projections, but fail to capture non-linear manifold geometry and produce dense, mixed-sign loadings that lack anatomical specificity.
To eliminate this transparency penalty without sacrificing representation capacity, we formulate Deep SiMLR (Similarity-driven Multi-view Reconstruction) deductively across five methodological stages governed by the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract: (1) restricting the input boundary of every modality to a linear projection on the compact Stiefel manifold (\(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\), \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) with Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) retraction, guaranteeing globally constant attribution derivatives (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m\)), closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)), and zero signed lobe crosstalk (\(\|\mathbf{V}_m^+ \odot \mathbf{V}_m^-\|_1 = 0\)); (2) coupling views via scale-profiled alignment energies, directed/bipartite consensus topologies (topology="graph"), and spectral Modality Alignment Index (MAI) triage; (3) optimizing linear multi-view Stiefel bases via first-order (SiMLR) and quasi-Newton (SiMLR-LBFGS, bound-constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB) Riemannian solvers that provide iteration-0 warm starts; (4) adding non-linear multi-layer perceptron decoding downstream of the linear encoder (LEND) without high-dimensional encoder overfitting (NED, NEDPP); and (5) composing \(\mathbf{V}_m\) with bijective RealNVP normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR-V) trained via detached-prior subspace decoupling (\(\text{sg}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}})\)), which we prove resolves rectangular Stiefel prior collapse onto trailing noise eigenvectors.
We benchmark nine architectures across 324 task evaluations spanning 12 multi-modal data regimes (six synthetic manifolds with known ground truth and six real-world clinical, multi-omics, and imaging cohorts: UCI Cleveland Heart Disease, Efron Diabetes Progression, 3-assay TCGA-BRCA, 3-assay TCGA-KIRC, 4-view ADNI-MCI, and 4-view UCI Multiple Features mfeat) across three independent seeds, alongside a 1,214-combination hyperparameter sweep and a 10-seed mediation benchmark on ADNI-MCI (\(N=1,084\)). Following Demšar’s block-level ranking protocol across the \(B = 12\) datasets, non-parametric inference confirms highly significant architectural separation across both consensus prediction (\(\chi_F^2 = 32.06, p = 9.10 \times 10^{-5}\); Iman–Davenport \(F_F = 5.51, p = 1.19 \times 10^{-5}\); Nemenyi \(CD = 3.468\)) and strictly linear OLEE basis probing (\(\chi_F^2 = 30.77, p = 1.54 \times 10^{-4}\); \(F_F = 5.19, p = 2.54 \times 10^{-5}\)). Hybrid LEND achieves the #1 global rank on consensus prediction (mean rank \(3.58\), mean score \(0.760 \pm 0.249\)) and the highest ground-truth latent recovery (\(CMC = 0.907\)). Bound-constrained quasi-Newton SiMLR-LBFGSB achieves the #1 global rank on the strictly linear OLEE basis probe (mean rank \(3.17\), #1 real-cohort rank \(2.50\), mean \(0.777\)) and the highest sparse support recovery (\(F_1 = 0.991\) vs. PCA \(0.333\)), while detached-prior Flow-SiMR-V ranks #3 overall (\(4.17\) consensus rank, \(4.12\) linear probe rank, #1 real-cohort consensus mean \(0.627\)) and NSAFlow-PCA executes in \(0.040\text{s}\) with \(25.0\%\) disjoint sparsity. Every OLEE-constrained model significantly outperforms unconstrained deep autoencoders (NED, NEDPP, \(p_{\text{Holm}} \le 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\)). In ADNI-MCI (\(N=1,084\)), aligning the three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) features) against the 11 \(>98\%\)-complete cognitive measures via a bipartite training graph (Protocol B) raises MRI-only out-of-sample cognitive factor prediction (CogPC1 R^2) to \(0.2237\) (SiMLR-LBFGSB 3-seed mean) and \(0.2407\) (SiMLR-Lookahead in our 1,214-combination sweep, with detached-prior Flow-SiMR-V reaching \(0.2341\) at \(k=3\) and \(0.2966\) at \(k=6\)) versus \(0.1522\) for PCA, while modeling the two-step cognitive mediation pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Cognition} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)) boosts out-of-sample prediction of clinical dementia severity over six-fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\) for LEND-SiMR + MAI; \(R^2 = 0.2443\) in \(0.86\text{s}\) for SiMLR; \(85\text{–}86\%\) indirect effect, \(p < 10^{-15}\)) vs. \(R^2 = 0.0411\) for direct MRI alone.

title: 1  Introduction and Background
text:
1.1 Introduction
High-throughput biomedical studies routinely collect multiple distinct measurements from each subject. In neurodegenerative disease research, cohorts such as the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008) and the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) (Marek et al. 2011) acquire structural MRI regional morphometry, diffusion tensor white matter fractional anisotropy, molecular PET, biofluid assays, and comprehensive psychometric batteries (Avants et al. 2014; Stone et al. 2020; Avants et al. 2021). In traumatic brain injury (TBI) and neurotrauma, blast-induced shockwave exposure produces diffuse axonal injury and non-local microstructural shearing that alter structural connectivity networks (Stone et al. 2024). In translational oncology, the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) profiles patient tumors across somatic copy-number alterations, transcriptomic expression, DNA methylation, and targeted reverse-phase protein arrays in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016) and clear cell renal cell carcinoma (KIRC) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013). Integrating these observations—formalized as \(M\) data matrices \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) for \(m = 1, \dots, M\) across \(n\) co-registered subjects—is essential for resolving phenotypic heterogeneity, identifying molecular subtypes, and mapping progression trajectories.
Deep representation learning methods, including Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (Deep CCA) (Andrew et al. 2013) and Multimodal Variational Autoencoders (MVAEs) (Wu and Goodman 2018), capture non-linear cross-modal dependencies. However, standard deep encoders map inputs through deeply nested affine transformations interleaved with non-linear activations (\(\mathbf{Z} = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_2 \sigma(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2)\)). This composition creates complex feature entanglement, obscuring the physical attribution between observable biological measurements and latent coordinates (Rudin 2019). In clinical diagnostics, oncology biomarker discovery, and neurotrauma assessment, this opacity imposes a severe transparency penalty: clinicians, regulatory agencies, and trial biostatisticians cannot determine whether a diagnostic score reflects authentic pathophysiology (such as entorhinal cortical atrophy or targeted kinase dysregulation) or idiosyncratic scanner noise and batch artifacts (Holmberg et al. 2022).
Post-hoc explainability techniques, such as LIME (Ribeiro et al. 2016) and SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017), attempt to infer feature importance by querying black-box models on randomly perturbed inputs. As demonstrated by Rudin (2019), post-hoc surrogates exhibit fundamental failure modes in biological domains. By perturbing features independently, they evaluate synthetic samples that violate physiological covariance—pairing, for example, incompatible regional brain volumes or mutually exclusive oncogenic mutations. Consequently, post-hoc explanations can be unstable, sensitive to hyperparameter tuning, and biologically deceptive (Radulovic 2023).
Conversely, classical linear dimensionality reduction methods—including Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling 1936)—provide exact linear loadings (\(Z_{jk} = \sum_i X_{ji} V_{ik}\)). Similarity-driven Multimodal Linear Reconstruction (SiMLR) (Avants et al. 2021) extended CCA to multiple modalities with sparsity and non-negativity constraints, solving a joint-variational problem on the Stiefel manifold. While linear SiMLR guarantees interpretability, complex disease processes can involve non-linear manifold geometry that linear projections cannot span. Furthermore, unconstrained PCA yields dense, mixed-sign loadings that lack anatomical specificity and fail to isolate shared cross-modal signals from modality-specific noise.

title: 1  Introduction and Background
text:
1.1.1 A Deductive Progression for Auditable Multi-View Integration
To resolve the tension between non-linear expressivity and auditable feature attribution, we construct Deep SiMLR deductively in five methodological stages (developed formally in Chapter 2 and evaluated stage-by-stage in Chapter 3):

Stage 1 — The Input Boundary (OLEE & NSA-Flow Manifold Geometry): Every modality enters through an Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) restricted to the compact Stiefel manifold: \[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \text{subject to } \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m) = \{\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k\}
\] Enforcing OLEE at the input boundary guarantees:

Globally Constant Attribution: \(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m\) (\(\partial Z_{m,ik} / \partial X_{m,ij} = V_{m,jk}\)), eliminating the black-box transparency penalty.
Closed-Form Counterfactual Recourse: Forward shifts (\(\Delta \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \Delta \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)) and minimal \(L_2\)-norm physical recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)) are exact orthogonal projections (Pearl 2009; Wachter et al. 2017).
Disjoint Non-Negative Support (nsa_flow): Retraction via the Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (NSAFlow-PCA, SiMLR-LBFGSB) minimizes the scale-invariant frame defect \(D(\mathbf{V}_m) = \|\mathbf{G}_m - \mathbf{I}_k / k\|_F^2\) while enforcing zero signed lobe crosstalk (\(\|\mathbf{V}_m^+ \odot \mathbf{V}_m^-\|_1 = 0\)).

Stage 2 — Cross-View Consensus, Bipartite Graph Topologies, and Spectral Triage (MAI): Per-view latents are fused via scale-profiled alignment energies (procrustes, nc, align, acc, logcosh), consensus mixing (pca, svd, ica, newton), and directed/bipartite consensus graphs (topology="graph"). When predictor views (\(m=1,\dots,M-1\)) are aligned to a training-only clinical target view (\(M\)) via a bipartite graph ({0:[3], 1:[3], 2:[3], 3:[0,1,2]}), the predictor bases \(\mathbf{V}_m\) are steered directly toward the clinical subspace without requiring clinical labels at test time. Dynamic Modality Alignment Index (MAI) gating down-weights uninformative views.
Stage 3 — Linear Multi-View Manifold Solvers & Iteration-0 Warm Start: We introduce first-order (SiMLR) and quasi-Newton (SiMLR-LBFGS, bound-constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB) Riemannian solvers on \(\prod_m \text{St}(k, p_m)\), which also serve as the Iteration-0 linear warm start for all downstream deep and flow architectures.
Stage 4 — Non-Linear Decoding Downstream of OLEE (LEND vs. NED / NEDPP): Keeping the encoder strictly linear (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)) while placing multi-layer perceptron capacity exclusively in the decoder (LEND) captures curved generative manifolds (\(g_m(\mathbf{U})\)) without suffering the high-dimensional encoder overfitting that collapses unconstrained deep encoders (NED, NEDPP) when \(p_m \gg n\).
Stage 5 — Bijective Normalizing Flows Downstream of OLEE (Flow-SiMR-V): Prepending \(\mathbf{V}_m\) to volume-preserving RealNVP coupling layers in \(\mathbb{R}^k\) provides exact analytical invertibility, conditional cross-view imputation, and geodesic trajectory mapping. Crucially, we prove that backpropagating standard Gaussian prior log-likelihood gradients (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} \mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}\)) through a rectangular Stiefel projection (\(k \ll p_m\)) drives \(\mathbf{V}_m\) onto the trailing (minimum-variance) eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{X}_m\), and we resolve this collapse via detached-prior subspace decoupling (\(\text{sg}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}})\)).



1.1.2 Multimodal Consensus as Latent Signal Recovery
We formalize multi-view integration as the estimation of a shared latent signal \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) from \(M\) observations: \[
\mathbf{X}_m = g_m(\mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{E}_m, \quad m = 1, \dots, M
\] where \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^{n \times k} \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) is a modality-specific generative mapping and \(\mathbf{E}_m\) represents domain-specific noise and private variance. Multi-modal consensus seeks mappings \(f_m(\mathbf{X}_m)\) that project each observation to a unified consensus representation \(\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) approximating \(\mathbf{S}\).
In biological cohorts, ambient feature dimensions often far exceed sample size (\(p_m \gg n\)). When a high-dimensional view contains little structured covariance, standard correlation objectives can capitalize on chance associations, corrupting the consensus space (Avants et al. 2025; Stone et al. 2024). Principled integration requires explicit regularization that penalizes off-manifold noise while preserving true biological signal.


1.1.3 Why Brain MRI Needs Bipartite Cognitive Alignment & Mediation in ADNI-MCI
A clear real-world example of why multi-view consensus topology (Stage 2) and a linear Stiefel entrypoint (Stage 1) matter comes from studying \(N = 1,084\) patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008). In clinical trials, the standard outcome used to judge whether a treatment works is the Clinical Dementia Rating – Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), alongside composite multi-domain cognitive performance (CogPC1, the primary latent axis across 11 \(>98\%\)-complete clinical and cognitive sub-scores from the ADAS-Cog, MMSE, Trails, FAQ, and RAVLT batteries after in-fold Frisch–Waugh–Lovell adjustment for age, sex, and education).
Each patient has four views of baseline data:

Three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) brain regions total): regional gray-matter volumes (\(p_1 = 160\)), hierarchical cortical surface thickness (\(p_2 = 160\)), and native T1-weighted cortical thickness (\(p_3 = 62\)).
One clinical/cognitive battery view (\(p_4 = 11\) items at \(>98\%\) completeness, or \(13\) items with MMSE/ADAS sub-items).

Evaluating how brain structure relates to cognition and daily disability on held-out test patients reveals four fundamental findings:

Predicting daily disability directly from brain MRI hits a biological ceiling (\(R^2 = 0.0411\)): When a model tries to predict CDR-SB directly from the 382 brain MRI measurements alone (Protocol A), it explains only \(4.1\%\) of the variance on unseen test patients (\(\text{Direct-Anatomy [SiMLR]}: R^2 = 0.0411 \pm 0.0248, \rho = 0.2203\)), and standard ridge regression on the concatenated MRI features fails (\(R^2 = -0.1810 \pm 0.0916\)). Even when predicting CogPC1 across the 11 complete cognitive tests, aligning the 3 MRI views only with each other (Protocol A, unsupervised 3-view star/LOO) reaches only \(R^2 \approx 0.15\text{–}0.17\) (PCA \(R^2 = 0.1522\); NSAFlow-PCA \(R^2 = 0.1592\)) because high-variance healthy anatomical covariance across the 382 MRI regions dominates the leading components.
Bipartite Graph Alignment (Protocol B: MRI Views \(\leftrightarrow\) Cognitive View During Training) Steers MRI Projections Toward the Disease Axis (\(R^2 = 0.224\text{–}0.241\) from MRI Alone): When the three MRI views (\(m \in \{0,1,2\}\)) are aligned directly against the cognitive view (\(m=3\)) during training via a bipartite graph (path_graph = {0:[3], 1:[3], 2:[3], 3:[0,1,2]})—and View 3 is completely withheld at test time so predictions use only the 3 MRI views’ linear projections \(\mathbf{X}_{m,\text{test}}\mathbf{V}_m\)—out-of-sample CogPC1 \(R^2\) rises to \(0.2237\) (SiMLR-LBFGSB, 3-seed mean in the global benchmark) and \(0.2407\) (SiMLR-Lookahead in our 1,214-combination hyperparameter sweep), outperforming single-matrix PCA (\(0.1522\)) by \(+47\%\) to \(+58\%\).
Modeling the Two-Step Mediation Pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Shared Cognitive Summary} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)) Boosts Disability Prediction Over 6-Fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\)): Tissue loss in the hippocampus or temporal cortex does not directly make a person unable to balance a checkbook; rather, brain atrophy first impairs cognitive test performance, and that cognitive decline drives trouble with daily activities. Aligning the three MRI views with the cognitive battery to form a mediated cognitive-anatomical summary increases out-of-sample CDR-SB accuracy more than six-fold:

\(\text{LEND-SiMR + MAI [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2648 \pm 0.0332\) (\(6.44\times\) higher than direct MRI, \(\rho = 0.5206\), paired Wilcoxon \(p = 9.77 \times 10^{-4}\) vs. covariates).
\(\text{SiMLR [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2443 \pm 0.0534\) (\(5.94\times\) higher than direct MRI, \(\rho = 0.4989\)) in just \(0.86\text{ seconds}\).
\(\text{Flow-SiMR-V + MAI [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2290 \pm 0.0696\) (\(5.57\times\) higher than direct MRI). Baron–Kenny and bootstrap mediation testing confirm that \(84.5\%\text{–}86.4\%\) of the effect of brain MRI atrophy on daily disability is indirect, acting through cognitive performance (\(p < 10^{-15}\)).

Unconstrained Deep Encoders Overfit the 382 MRI Features and Collapse on Test Patients (\(R^2 = 0.1127\)): Replacing the linear Stiefel entrypoint with an unconstrained multi-layer perceptron encoder on the mediated pathway cuts test-set accuracy by more than half (\(\text{NED-SiMR + MAI [Mediated]}: R^2 = 0.1127 \pm 0.0578\); \(\text{NED-Shared-Private}: R^2 = 0.0840 \pm 0.0412\)). Restricting the first layer to an orthonormal linear projection (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) acts as an essential geometric safeguard against high-dimensional overfitting while keeping every brain region’s weight directly readable.

1.2 Background

1.2.1 Subspace Invariance versus Basis Axis Sensitivity
When evaluating multi-view representations, it is essential to distinguish between the subspace spanned by a projection and the individual coordinate axes:

Subspace Invariance: For any orthogonal transformation \(\mathbf{M} \in O(k)\), the rotated representation \(\mathbf{Z}_m \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{X}_m (\mathbf{V}_m \mathbf{M})\) spans the identical linear subspace as \(\mathbf{Z}_m\). Unregularized linear regression models trained on \(\mathbf{Z}_m \mathbf{M}\) achieve identical predictions to those trained on \(\mathbf{Z}_m\).
Basis Localization & Sparse Support Recovery: Identifying individual anatomical or molecular biomarkers requires that specific coordinate axes localize onto distinct biological feature blocks rather than mixing them across arbitrary orthogonal rotations. Whereas unregularized linear probes depend only on \(\text{span}(\mathbf{V}_m)\), direct sparse support overlap (\(F_1\) / Jaccard recovery) and sparsity metrics depend directly on the coordinate orientation and sparsity of \(\mathbf{V}_m\).
Signed Support Disjointness: In non-negative or contrast-split representations (\(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}^+ - \mathbf{V}^-\) with \(\mathbf{V}^+, \mathbf{V}^- \ge 0\)), overlap between positive and negative lobes produces destructive cancellation. Enforcing disjoint support (\(\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^- = \mathbf{0}\)) eliminates crosstalk, ensuring that positive and negative coefficients index distinct feature sets.

Figure 1.1: Architectural Comparison of the Interpretability Gap. Unconstrained deep multi-view encoders entangle input features across hidden layers, requiring post-hoc perturbation surrogates (SHAP/LIME). The Stiefel-constrained Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) enforces an orthonormal linear basis \(\mathbf{V}_m\) (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) at the input boundary, guaranteeing exact constant attribution (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m}\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)) prior to downstream non-linear decoding or normalizing flows.





1.2.2 Architectural Taxonomy Organized by Deductive Stage
We evaluate nine distinct architectures spanning single-matrix baselines, linear multi-view Stiefel solvers, hybrid OLEE autoencoders, unconstrained deep autoencoders, and bijective normalizing flows:

Stage 1 Single-Matrix Baselines (PCA, NSAFlow-PCA):

PCA (Classical Linear Baseline): Standard Principal Component Analysis fitted via singular value decomposition on concatenated, standardized predictor views (\(\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}_1 \dots \mathbf{X}_M]\)). Establishes the unconstrained dense linear baseline (\(0.043\text{s}\)).
NSAFlow-PCA (Accelerated Non-negative Stiefel Flow): A fast single-matrix manifold solver utilizing direct SVD initialization on concatenated features and differentiable Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) retraction in \(0.040\text{s}\) with \(25.0\%\) disjoint sparsity.

Stage 3 Linear Multi-View Manifold Solvers (SiMLR, SiMLR-LBFGS, SiMLR-LBFGSB):

SiMLR (Riemannian Gradient Descent): The classical linear cross-view formulation solving the multi-view alignment problem via Armijo line-search gradient descent with per-sweep NSA-Flow retraction (\(0.556\text{s}\)).
SiMLR-LBFGS (Quasi-Newton Riemannian): A linear cross-view architecture incorporating two-loop L-BFGS curvature steps on the Stiefel manifold with per-sweep NSA-Flow retraction (\(\text{Support } F_1 = 0.966\)).
SiMLR-LBFGSB (Bound-Constrained Quasi-Newton): A linear cross-view architecture using the NSA-Flow bound-constrained L-BFGS-B solver (nsa_lbfgsb), enforcing \(\mathbf{V}_m \ge \mathbf{0}\) inside the quasi-Newton step when positivity is active (\(\text{Support } F_1 = 0.991\)).

Stage 4 Non-Linear Decoding vs. Deep Encoding (LEND, NED, NEDPP):

LEND (Linear Encoder, Non-linear Decoder): A hybrid OLEE architecture coupling per-view linear Stiefel projections (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)) with a multi-layer perceptron decoder for non-linear feature reconstruction and cross-view consensus alignment.
NED (Non-linear Encoder-Decoder): A deep architecture adding hidden non-linear encoder layers after the initial linear projection (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = f_{\text{enc},m}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m)\)).
NEDPP (Shared and Private Subspaces): An extension of NED that partitions latent coordinates into shared consensus and view-specific private subspaces using cross-covariance penalties.

Stage 5 Bijective Normalizing Flows (Flow-SiMR-V):

Flow-SiMR-V (Bijective Normalizing Flow with Stiefel Bottleneck): An invertible OLEE architecture prepending a linear Stiefel projection matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m\) to volume-preserving RealNVP affine coupling layers in \(\mathbb{R}^k\) trained with detached-prior subspace decoupling, enabling continuous density estimation, exact invertibility, and conditional cross-view imputation.




1.2.3 Summary of Contributions

The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) Contract & NSA-Flow Geometry (Stage 1): We formalize how restricting the input layer of multi-view encoders to the compact Stiefel manifold eliminates the clinical transparency penalty (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and enables closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top\), connecting directly to Pearl (2009) and Wachter et al. (2017)) while enforcing exact zero signed lobe crosstalk (\(\|\mathbf{V}_m^+ \odot \mathbf{V}_m^-\|_1 = 0\)).
Bipartite Consensus Topologies & ADNI-MCI Cognitive Mediation (Stage 2): Across a 1,214-combination sweep on ADNI-MCI (\(N = 1,084\)), we demonstrate why aligning structural MRI views with a training-only cognitive battery via a bipartite graph (Protocol B) boosts out-of-sample cognitive factor prediction (CogPC1 R^2 \(= 0.224\text{–}0.241\) vs. PCA \(0.152\)), and how modeling the two-step mediation pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Cognition} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)) increases daily disability prediction over 6-fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\) for LEND-SiMR + MAI; \(R^2 = 0.2443\) in \(0.86\text{s}\) for SiMLR; \(85\text{–}86\%\) indirect effect, \(p < 10^{-15}\)).
Bound-Constrained Quasi-Newton Manifold Optimization (SiMLR-LBFGSB, SiMLR-LBFGS, Stage 3): We show that coupling L-BFGS-B / L-BFGS optimization with NSA-Flow retractions achieves the top global Friedman rank on the strictly linear OLEE basis probe (\(3.17\) for SiMLR-LBFGSB, \(4.00\) for SiMLR-LBFGS; real-cohort ranks \(2.50\) and \(3.33\)) and near-exact sparse ground-truth support recovery (\(0.991\) and \(0.966\) vs. PCA \(0.333\)).
Hybrid Linear-Encoder Deep Decoding (LEND, Stage 4): We demonstrate that pairing an auditable linear encoder with a non-linear MLP decoder achieves the #1 global Friedman rank on consensus prediction (\(3.58\), mean \(0.760 \pm 0.249\)), the highest ground-truth latent recovery (\(CMC = 0.907\)), and a decisive advantage when views carry strong view-private noise (Shared+Private: \(R^2 = 0.949\) vs. PCA \(0.639\)) or weak sparse parts (NonnegPartsWeak: \(R^2 = 0.732\) vs. PCA \(0.522\)).
Resolution of Rectangular OLEE Prior Collapse in Flow-SiMR-V (Stage 5): We prove why backpropagating Gaussian prior log-likelihood gradients into a rectangular Stiefel basis (\(k \ll p_m\)) collapses \(\mathbf{V}_m\) onto trailing noise eigenvectors, and show that detached-prior subspace decoupling raises Flow-SiMR-V performance by \(+704\%\) on ADNI-MCI (CogPC1 R^2 from \(0.0369\) to \(0.2966\) / \(0.2341\)) and to #3 overall rank across all 12 benchmark datasets.
Rigorous 12-Dataset Non-Parametric Demšar Benchmark & 4-Axis Pareto Frontier: Across 324 task evaluations (12 data regimes—6 synthetic manifolds and 6 real clinical/multi-omics/imaging cohorts—\(\times\) 3 independent seeds \(\times\) 9 models), we conduct block-level Friedman (\(\chi_F^2 = 30.77\text{–}32.06, p \le 1.54 \times 10^{-4}\)), Iman–Davenport (\(F_F = 5.19\text{–}5.51, p \le 2.54 \times 10^{-5}\)), and Wilcoxon–Holm tests, mapping the 4-axis Pareto frontier across predictive accuracy, latent/support recovery, geometric invariants, and wall-clock latency.

2.1 Stage 1: The Input Boundary — OLEE and NSA-Flow Manifold Geometry
We develop the Deep SiMLR framework deductively in five progressive stages. Each stage addresses a structural limitation of the preceding one while preserving exact physical auditability at the input boundary:

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1.1 The Multi-Modal Inverse Problem
We frame multi-modal representation learning as a structured inverse problem over \(M\) distinct observational domains. Let \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) denote the centered observation matrix for modality \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), where \(n\) is the number of co-registered subjects and \(p_m\) is the ambient feature dimensionality. Each modality provides a partial, noisy observation of an underlying shared latent biological state \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) governed by modality-specific forward generative processes: \[
\mathbf{X}_m = g_m(\mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{E}_m
\tag{2.1}\] where \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\) is a smooth generative map applied row-wise across observations, and \(\mathbf{E}_m\) represents domain-specific observational noise and idiosyncratic view-private variance. The objective is to estimate an auditable coordinate representation of \(\mathbf{S}\) while isolating cross-modal consensus from view-private noise.


2.1.2 The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) as a Structural Information Bottleneck
Standard deep autoencoders and multi-layer perceptrons process inputs via unconstrained compositions \(\mathbf{Z} = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{X})\). Following Tishby’s Information Bottleneck principle (Tishby et al. 2000), unconstrained deep encoders entangle features across successive layers, readily memorizing high-dimensional noise and structured nuisance variables when \(p_m \sim n\). In biomedical discovery, this produces representation collapse on held-out subjects and obscures physical feature attribution (Rudin 2019).
We resolve this entanglement at the architectural boundary by enforcing the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract. OLEE mandates that the initial transformation of any modality \(\mathbf{X}_m\) is a linear projection onto the compact Stiefel manifold \(\text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k \}\) (Edelman et al. 1998; Boumal 2023): \[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}, \quad \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m), \quad \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k
\tag{2.2}\] Because the intrinsic dimension is strictly bounded (\(k \ll p_m\)) and \(\mathbf{V}_m\) acts as a partial isometry, OLEE imposes a geometric information bottleneck at the input boundary: \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m), \quad \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k
\tag{2.3}\] All subsequent non-linear operations (decoders, prediction heads, or normalizing flows) consume \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\), never raw features \(\mathbf{X}_m\). This structural contract yields three exact mathematical guarantees:

Exact Feature Attribution & Constant Input Gradient: The latent score \(z_{i, l}\) for subject \(i\) on component \(l\) is strictly the linear inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^{p_m} X_{i, j} V_{j, l}\). The directional derivative of the first-layer representation with respect to input observations is globally constant across the entire domain: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m
\tag{2.4}\] Because this input Jacobian is independent of \(\mathbf{X}_m\), the attribution profile is invariant across subjects, eliminating gradient saturation and post-hoc surrogate sampling artifacts (Lundberg and Lee 2017; Radulovic 2023).
Global Variance Partitioning: Because \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\), the projection is an isometry on \(\mathbb{R}^k\), and projected variance decomposes additively across orthogonal axes: \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}) = \sum_{l=1}^k \text{Var}(\mathbf{z}_{m, l})\).
Closed-Form Minimum-Norm Counterfactuals: Targeted counterfactual state transitions can be evaluated analytically in closed form without iterative gradient search, as established by the following theorem.


2.1.2.1 Theorem: Closed-Form Minimum-Norm Counterfactuals
Theorem:
Let a subject have latent representation \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^k\) under the OLEE basis \(\mathbf{V} \in \text{St}(k, p)\). To transition the subject to a targeted counterfactual latent state \(\mathbf{z}^* = \mathbf{z} + \Delta \mathbf{z}\), the unique perturbation \(\delta \mathbf{x}^* \in \mathbb{R}^p\) that minimizes the Euclidean intervention effort \(\|\delta \mathbf{x}\|_2^2\) while satisfying \((\mathbf{x} + \delta \mathbf{x}) \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{z}^*\) is given analytically by: \[
\delta \mathbf{x}^* = \Delta \mathbf{z} \mathbf{V}^\top
\tag{2.5}\]
Proof:
The counterfactual perturbation problem is formulated as the constrained optimization: \[
\min_{\delta \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^p} \frac{1}{2} \|\delta \mathbf{x}\|_2^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} = \Delta \mathbf{z}
\tag{2.6}\] Introducing Lagrange multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^k\), the Lagrangian is: \[
\mathcal{L}(\delta \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \frac{1}{2} \delta \mathbf{x} \delta \mathbf{x}^\top - (\delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} - \Delta \mathbf{z}) \boldsymbol{\lambda}
\] Setting the gradient with respect to \(\delta \mathbf{x}\) to zero gives \(\nabla_{\delta \mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L} = \delta \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{V}^\top = \mathbf{0} \implies \delta \mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{V}^\top\). Multiplying on the right by \(\mathbf{V}\) and using \(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k\) yields \(\delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} = \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{I}_k = \Delta \mathbf{z}\), whence \(\delta \mathbf{x}^* = \Delta \mathbf{z} \mathbf{V}^\top\). \(\square\)



2.1.3 Scale-Invariant Frame Defect, Angle Defect, and Signed Support Consolidation
An unconstrained orthonormal basis on \(\text{St}(k, p_m)\) is still dense and mixed-sign: every feature loads on every component, and positive and negative weights cancel within each column. To interpolate smoothly between dense orthogonal projections and sparse, disjoint, non-negative feature clusters, we regularize \(\mathbf{V}_m\) via Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) (Avants et al. 2025).

2.1.3.1 Trace-Normalized Stiefel Frame Defect (\(D\))
The trace-normalized frame defect (src/pysimlr/utils.py:504-630) measures departure from equal-norm column orthonormality: \[
D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{1}{1 - 1/k} \left\| \frac{\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}}{\text{tr}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})} - \frac{1}{k} \mathbf{I}_k \right\|_F^2
\tag{2.7}\] Let \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) and \(t = \text{tr}(\mathbf{G}) = \|\mathbf{V}\|_F^2\). Writing \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}} = \mathbf{G} / t\), the Frobenius norm expands into off-diagonal column decorrelation plus diagonal norm balance: \[
\left\|\tilde{\mathbf{G}} - \frac{1}{k} \mathbf{I}_k\right\|_F^2 = \sum_{i \ne j} \tilde{G}_{ij}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^k \left( \tilde{G}_{ii} - \frac{1}{k} \right)^2
\] Because the participation ratio is \(\text{EffRank}(\mathbf{V}) = t^2 / \|\mathbf{G}\|_F^2\), the defect connects directly to effective rank: \(D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{1}{1 - 1/k} \left( \frac{1}{\text{EffRank}(\mathbf{V})} - \frac{1}{k} \right)\). Differentiating with respect to \(\mathbf{V}\) yields: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}} D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{4}{t^2 (1 - 1/k)} \left[ \mathbf{V} \mathbf{G} - \frac{\|\mathbf{G}\|_F^2}{t} \mathbf{V} \right]
\tag{2.8}\] By Euler’s theorem for degree-0 homogeneous functions, \(\langle \nabla_{\mathbf{V}} D(\mathbf{V}), \mathbf{V} \rangle \equiv 0\), so \(D(\mathbf{V})\) exerts zero radial force on matrix scale.


2.1.3.2 Squared-Cosine Angle Defect (\(C\))
When biological components have unequal norms, we also evaluate the column-scale-invariant squared-cosine angle defect (angle_defect in src/pysimlr/utils.py:633-724), with \(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{V} \text{diag}(\|\mathbf{v}_1\|_2^{-1}, \dots, \|\mathbf{v}_k\|_2^{-1})\): \[
C(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{\|\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U} - \mathbf{I}_k\|_F^2}{k(k - 1)}
\tag{2.9}\] with gradient: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}} C(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{4}{k(k - 1)} \left[ \mathbf{U} \mathbf{H} - \mathbf{U} \, \text{diag}\left(\text{rowsum}(\mathbf{H}^{\odot 2})\right) \right] \text{diag}(\|\mathbf{v}_1\|_2^{-1}, \dots, \|\mathbf{v}_k\|_2^{-1}), \quad \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U} - \mathbf{I}_k
\tag{2.10}\] For non-negative matrices \(\mathbf{V} \ge \mathbf{0}\) with non-zero columns, \(C(\mathbf{V}) = 0\) if and only if the columns have pairwise disjoint supports.


2.1.3.3 Direct SVD Contrast Splitting and Support Consolidation
To represent bidirectional biological responses (e.g., cortical atrophy vs. ventricular expansion) without sign cancellation, we lift each basis \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times k}\) into paired non-negative lobes: \[
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}^+ - \mathbf{V}^-, \quad \mathbf{V}^+ = \max(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{0}), \quad \mathbf{V}^- = \max(-\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{0})
\tag{2.11}\] forming \(\mathbf{W} = [\mathbf{V}^+ \mid \mathbf{V}^-] \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{p \times 2k}\), initialized via Direct SVD Contrast Splitting: \[
\mathbf{E} = \text{SVD}_k(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathbf{W}_0 = [\max(\mathbf{E}, \mathbf{0}) \mid \max(-\mathbf{E}, \mathbf{0})]
\tag{2.12}\] When strict disjoint assignment is requested (consolidate=True), the deterministic support consolidation operator assigns each feature \(j\) to its winning lobe: \[
\text{win}(j) = \arg\max_{l \in \{1, \dots, 2k\}} W_{j, l}
\tag{2.13}\] guaranteeing exact zero lobe crosstalk (\(\|\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^-\|_1 = 0\)).



2.1.4 Subspace Invariance vs. Sparse Basis Localization
Evaluating whether a method recovered the right basis requires distinguishing the linear subspace \(\text{span}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V})\) from the individual columns of \(\mathbf{V}\).

2.1.4.1 Theorem: Rotation Invariance of Linear Subspace Probes
Theorem:
Let \(\mathbf{Z}_1 = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) and let \(\mathbf{M} \in \text{GL}(k, \mathbb{R})\) be any invertible \(k \times k\) matrix defining an alternative basis \(\mathbf{Z}_2 = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}\). For any regression target \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\):

The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) projection hat matrices are identical: \(\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} \equiv \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_1}\).
The fitted values and regression \(R^2\) are strictly invariant: \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2 \equiv \hat{\mathbf{y}}_1\) and \(R^2(\mathbf{Z}_2, \mathbf{y}) \equiv R^2(\mathbf{Z}_1, \mathbf{y})\).

Proof:
The OLS hat matrix projecting \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the column space of \(\mathbf{Z}_2\) is: \[
\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} = \mathbf{Z}_2 \left( \mathbf{Z}_2^\top \mathbf{Z}_2 \right)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}_2^\top
\tag{2.14}\] Substituting \(\mathbf{Z}_2 = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}\) and using \((\mathbf{A} \mathbf{B} \mathbf{C})^{-1} = \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{B}^{-1} \mathbf{A}^{-1}\) for invertible \(\mathbf{M}\) yields \(\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M} \mathbf{M}^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_1^\top \mathbf{Z}_1)^{-1} (\mathbf{M}^\top)^{-1} \mathbf{M}^\top \mathbf{Z}_1^\top = \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_1}\). \(\square\)
Consequently, we evaluate representations across both linear probes—the Strictly Linear OLEE Basis Probe (\(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\)) and the Global Consensus Probe (\(\mathbf{U}\))—together with Ground-Truth Support Recovery (\(\text{Support } F_1\) on \(\mathbf{V}\)) and Canonical Mean Correlation (\(CMC\) on \(\mathbf{U}\)), which directly measure whether \(\mathbf{V}_m\) localizes true disjoint feature clusters and whether \(\mathbf{U}\) recovers the underlying latent coordinates.

section: 2.2 Stage 2: Cross-View Consensus — Mixing, Graph Topologies, and Spectral Triage
text:
2.2 Stage 2: Cross-View Consensus — Mixing, Graph Topologies, and Spectral Triage
Given per-modality latent representations \(\mathbf{Z}_m = f_m(\mathbf{X}_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) and decoders \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\), the global joint-variational functional couples within-modality reconstruction fidelity, cross-modal alignment against a modality-specific consensus target \(\mathbf{U}_m\), and manifold regularization: \[
\min_{\{f_m, g_m\}_{m=1}^M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{X}_m, g_m(\mathbf{Z}_m)) + \lambda_{\text{sim}} w_m \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}(\mathbf{Z}_m, \mathbf{U}_m) + \gamma D(\mathbf{V}_m) \right] + \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Z})
\tag{2.15}\]

2.2.1 Consensus Topologies: star, loo, and Directed/Bipartite graph
How the target \(\mathbf{U}_m\) is constructed from the set of modality projections \(\{\mathbf{Z}_j\}_{j=1}^M\) governs what shared structure the bases \(\mathbf{V}_m\) learn:

Global Star Topology (topology="star"): Every modality aligns to a single pooled consensus \(\mathbf{U} = \text{Consensus}(\{\mathbf{Z}_j\}_{j=1}^M)\). In high-capacity models, including \(\mathbf{Z}_m\) inside its own target allows modality \(m\) to partially satisfy the alignment objective through self-correlation.
Leave-One-Out Topology (topology="loo"): Modality \(m\) aligns strictly against the consensus of all other modalities: \[
\mathbf{U}_{\neq m} = \text{Consensus}\left( \{\mathbf{Z}_j\}_{j \neq m} \right)
\tag{2.16}\] quarantining modality \(m\) from contributing to its own target and preventing self-memorization.
Directed / Bipartite Graph Topology (topology="graph", path_graph) and Partial-View Test Inference:
In many clinical and biological studies, \(M-1\) predictor views \(\{\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_{M-1}\}\) (such as three structural brain MRI views or three multi-omics assays) are available both during training and at deployment, whereas a \(M\)-th clinical or phenotypic target view \(\mathbf{X}_M = \mathbf{Y}_{\text{clin}}\) (such as a multi-domain cognitive battery) is observed during training but withheld at test time.
When the predictor views are aligned only with each other (Protocol A), their cross-view covariance is dominated by high-variance background anatomy or housekeeping biology rather than the clinical phenotype. By specifying a bipartite adjacency graph \(\mathcal{G}\) connecting each predictor view \(m \in \{1, \dots, M-1\}\) exclusively to the target view \(M\): \[
\mathbf{U}_m = \text{Consensus}(\{\mathbf{Z}_M\}) \quad (m = 1, \dots, M-1), \qquad \mathbf{U}_M = \text{Consensus}\left(\{\mathbf{Z}_1, \dots, \mathbf{Z}_{M-1}\}\right)
\tag{2.17}\] every predictor basis \(\mathbf{V}_m\) is steered directly toward the clinical subspace during training. At test time, View \(M\) is withheld (eval_view_indices \(= \{1, \dots, M-1\}\)) and out-of-sample latent coordinates are computed strictly from the predictor views’ OLEE projections: \[
\hat{\mathbf{U}}_{\text{test}} = \frac{1}{M - 1} \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} \mathbf{X}_{m,\text{test}} \mathbf{V}_m
\tag{2.18}\] This bipartite training / partial-view testing protocol requires zero test labels while preventing healthy anatomical covariance among the predictor views from swamping the disease-relevant subspace.



2.2.2 Scale-Profiled Alignment Energies (procrustes, recon_r2, align, acc, logcosh)
The alignment functional \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}(\mathbf{Z}_m, \mathbf{U}_m)\) must be scale-well-posed so it cannot be trivially minimized by shrinking \(\|\mathbf{V}_m\|_F \to 0\):

Scale-Profiled Procrustes & Cosine Alignment (procrustes, align, acc): Measures orthogonal Procrustes similarity \(-\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_m^\top \tilde{\mathbf{U}}_m)\) or normalized trace correlation \(-\text{tr}(\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_m^\top \tilde{\mathbf{U}}_m)\) on Frobenius-normalized projections.
Scale-Profiled Reconstruction \(R^2\) (recon_r2): Profiles out optimal linear scaling before measuring residual variance, eliminating the zero-basis trap of unnormalized regression MSE.
Robust Log-Cosh Negentropy (logcosh): To bound the influence of heavy-tailed clinical outliers (calculate_ica_energy in src/pysimlr/simlr.py:844-848), we evaluate: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{log-cosh}}(\mathbf{Z}_m, \mathbf{U}_{m}) = - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^k \left( |C_{ji}| - \log 2 + \log\left(1 + e^{-2|C_{ji}|}\right) \right), \quad \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{U}_m^\top \mathbf{Z}_m
\tag{2.19}\] whose first-order variational gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{V}_m\) has strictly bounded leverage (\(|\tanh(C_{ji})| < 1\)): \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} \mathcal{L}_{\text{log-cosh}} = - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{U}_{m} \tanh(\mathbf{C})
\tag{2.20}\]



2.2.3 Sign-Aligned Consensus Mixing (pca, svd, ica, newton)
Latent factorizations are invariant under coordinate sign reflections (\(\mathbf{z}_j \leftrightarrow -\mathbf{z}_j\)). When two views recover the same biological factor with opposite signs, naive cross-modal averaging suffers destructive cancellation: \[
\bar{\mathbf{u}}_l = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum_{j \ne m} \mathbf{z}_{j, l} \approx \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u}_l - \mathbf{u}_l) = \mathbf{0}
\tag{2.21}\] Prior to mixing (align_column_signs in src/pysimlr/utils.py:2003-2064), we synchronize column signs greedily against the running coordinate sum \(\mathbf{R}\): \[
s_{j, l} = \text{sign}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n Z_{j, il} R_{il} \right), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j = \mathbf{Z}_j \, \text{diag}(s_{j, 1}, \dots, s_{j, k}), \quad \mathbf{R} \leftarrow \mathbf{R} + \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j
\tag{2.22}\] From the sign-aligned projections \(\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j\), pysimlr supports two families of consensus mixing: 1. Sign-Aligned Mean + Gram–Schmidt (mixing_algorithm="pca") and Spectral Concatenation ("svd", "ica"): Particularly effective for linear manifold solvers where exact block coordinate updates are taken at each iteration. 2. Differentiable Newton–Schulz Polar Mixing (mixing_algorithm="newton"): Computes the closest column-orthogonal consensus via 10 cubic Newton–Schulz iterations without GPU-serializing SVD calls or discontinuous singular-vector sign flips across mini-batches: \[
   \bar{\mathbf{U}}_{m} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(m)|} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(m)} \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j, \qquad \mathbf{U}_{m} = \text{NewtonSchulz}\left( \bar{\mathbf{U}}_{m}, \text{iterations}=10 \right)
    \tag{2.23}\] with exponential moving-average anchor sign synchronization across mini-batch epochs: \[
   \mathbf{A}^{(t)} = 0.9 \, \mathbf{A}^{(t-1)} + 0.1 \left( \mathbf{A}_{\text{new}} \odot \text{signs} \right)
    \tag{2.24}\]


2.2.4 Spectral Triage and the Modality Alignment Index (MAI)
When integrating \(M \ge 3\) heterogeneous views, an uninformative or corrupted modality can pull the consensus toward isotropic noise. Under the Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP) phase transition (Baik et al. 2005), informative modalities exhibit leading singular values that escape the Marchenko–Pastur bulk, whereas pure noise views remain flat (Figure 2.1).








Figure 2.1: Spectral Sharpness as a Discriminant of Modality Fidelity. Informative modalities (green) exhibit leading singular values that escape the Marchenko-Pastur bulk (gray span), whereas isotropic noise modalities (orange) remain trapped within the bulk limit.





In both linear (simlr) and deep/flow models (lend_simr, ned_simr, flow_simr, flow_simr_v), we score each modality \(m\) against its Leave-One-Out consensus \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\) via Scale-Profiled Procrustes \(R^2\) (or canonical correlation cca / RV-coefficient rvcoef): \[
R_m^2 = \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(\tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_m^\top \tilde{\mathbf{U}}_{\neq m}) \right)^2 \in [0, 1]
\tag{2.25}\] optionally modulated by spectral sharpness \(\mathcal{S}_m = \sigma_1(\mathbf{Z}_m) / \sum_{j=1}^k \sigma_j(\mathbf{Z}_m)\) (mai_metric="procrustes_r2_sharp"): \[
\text{MAI}_m = R_m^2 \cdot \mathcal{S}_m
\tag{2.26}\] (Note: When \(M = 2\), Leave-One-Out compares View 1 to View 2 and View 2 to View 1 with a symmetric spectrum, so \(\text{MAI}_1 \equiv \text{MAI}_2\) and weights remain uniform \([0.5, 0.5]\); MAI triage is therefore specifically a property of \(M \ge 3\) views.)
The raw alignment indices are smoothed via EMA and passed through a mean-centered sigmoid gate with linear warmup: \[
\mathbf{mai}^{(t)} = 0.9 \, \mathbf{mai}^{(t-1)} + 0.1 \, \mathbf{mai}_{\text{raw}}^{(t)}
\tag{2.27}\] \[
\omega_m^{\text{gate}} = \sigma\left( \kappa \cdot (\text{mai}_m^{(t)} - \mu_{\text{mai}}) \right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\kappa (\text{mai}_m^{(t)} - \mu_{\text{mai}})\right)}
\tag{2.28}\] \[
\tilde{w}_m = \text{mai}_m^{(t)} \cdot \omega_m^{\text{gate}}, \quad w_m^{\text{target}} = \frac{\tilde{w}_m}{\sum_{j=1}^M \tilde{w}_j + 10^{-8}}
\tag{2.29}\] \[
\mathbf{w}^{(t)} = (1 - \rho) \mathbf{w}_{\text{uniform}} + \rho \mathbf{w}^{\text{target}}
\tag{2.30}\] While simple averaging across \(M\) views reduces independent noise at rate \(1/M\), correlated cross-modal artifacts leave an irreducible floor bounded by the cross-view noise correlation \(\rho_{\text{noise}}\): \[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{U}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{M} (1 - \rho_{\text{noise}}) + \rho_{\text{noise}} \sigma^2
\tag{2.31}\] which LOO/bipartite topologies and MAI actively suppress.

2.3.1 Iteration-0 Warm-Start Calibration
A critical numerical invariant in alternating manifold optimization is Iteration-0 Warm-Start Calibration (src/pysimlr/simlr.py:1512-1606). When bases \(\{\mathbf{V}_m^{(0)}\}\) are initialized via per-view SVD/PCA or GCCA, the initial projections \(\mathbf{Z}_m^{(0)} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m^{(0)}\) already span a high-variance subspace. Evaluating the initial consensus \(\mathbf{U}^{(0)}\), calibrating the relative modality normalization weights normalizing_weights and orth_weights, and recording init_total_energy at iteration \(t = 0\) prior to the first gradient step ensures that the initial step size is properly scaled and that best_v_mats can never degrade below the warm-start initialization.


2.3.2 Riemannian Tangent Projection, Sylvester Polar Factor, and Newton–Schulz Retraction
For each basis \(\mathbf{V} \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\): \[
\text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k \}
\tag{2.32}\] the tangent space and Riemannian gradient projection (project_gradient in src/pysimlr/simlr.py:111-146) are: \[
T_{\mathbf{V}} \text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \Delta + \Delta^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{0} \}
\tag{2.33}\] \[
\Pi_{T_{\mathbf{V}}}(\mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{G} - \mathbf{V} \, \text{sym}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{G} - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{V} (\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{G} + \mathbf{G}^\top \mathbf{V})
\tag{2.34}\] To map an updated iterate \(\mathbf{Y}\) back to \(\text{St}(k, p_m)\) via the polar factor: \[
R(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{Y} (\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y})^{-1/2}
\tag{2.35}\] without differentiating through torch.linalg.svd (whose backward pass divides by \(\sigma_i^2 - \sigma_j^2\) and produces NaN at repeated singular values \(\sigma_i = 1\)), pysimlr uses nsa_flow.polar_factor, which differentiates \(\mathbf{H} = (\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y})^{1/2}\) via the continuous Lyapunov/Sylvester equation: \[
\mathbf{H} (d\mathbf{H}) + (d\mathbf{H}) \mathbf{H} = (d\mathbf{Y})^\top \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{Y}^\top (d\mathbf{Y})
\tag{2.36}\] or applies the matrix-multiplication-only cubic Newton–Schulz recurrence: \[
\mathbf{Y}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{Y}}{\|\mathbf{Y}\|_F}, \quad \mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{Y}_\tau \left( 3 \mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{Y}_\tau^\top \mathbf{Y}_\tau \right)
\tag{2.37}\] whose singular value errors \(\epsilon_{\tau, i} = 1 - \sigma_{\tau, i}\) contract quadratically for \(\sigma_{0, i} \in (0, \sqrt{3})\): \[
\|\mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1}^\top \mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1} - \mathbf{I}_k\| = \mathcal{O}\left(\|\mathbf{Y}_\tau^\top \mathbf{Y}_\tau - \mathbf{I}_k\|^2\right)
\tag{2.38}\] \[
\epsilon_{\tau+1, i} = 1 - \sigma_{\tau+1, i} = \frac{3}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 - \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^3 = \epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 \left( \frac{3 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}}{2} \right)
\tag{2.39}\] as illustrated geometrically in Figure 2.3.








Figure 2.3: Geometrical Intuition of Orthogonal Discovery via Stiefel Retraction. Unconstrained optimization allows latent components to collapse onto the dominant variance direction (left, red vectors), whereas Stiefel/NSA-Flow retractions maintain orthogonal, non-redundant axes (right, green vectors).







2.3.3 Quasi-Newton Curvature Steps (SiMLR-LBFGS and Bound-Constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB)
First-order optimizers (armijo_gradient, lars, adam, hybrid_adam) canzig-zag across narrow ravines formed by cross-view alignment and orthogonality penalties. We provide two second-order quasi-Newton linear solvers:

SiMLR-LBFGS (optimizer_type="torch_lbfgs"): Uses two-loop inverse-Hessian recursion with Strong Wolfe line search and an analytical gradient closure (src/pysimlr/optimizers.py:841-894): \[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t + \alpha_t \mathbf{p}_t) \le \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t) + c_1 \alpha_t \text{tr}(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)^\top \mathbf{p}_t)
\tag{2.40}\]
SiMLR-LBFGSB (optimizer_type="nsa_lbfgsb"): Uses the bound-constrained L-BFGS-B solver from nsa_flow, enforcing non-negativity (\(\mathbf{V}_m \ge \mathbf{0}\)) directly inside the active-set quasi-Newton subspace step rather than by post-hoc clipping.

2.4 Stage 4: Non-Linear Decoding Downstream of OLEE (LEND vs. NED and NEDPP)
When the generative mapping \(\mathbf{X}_m = g_m(\mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{E}_m\) is non-linear, a linear decoder \(g_m(\mathbf{Z}_m) = \mathbf{Z}_m \mathbf{W}_m\) cannot reconstruct curved manifold trajectories. However, replacing the encoder with an unconstrained MLP destroys the constant attribution guarantee \(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m}\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\) and risks memorizing high-dimensional noise when \(p_m \sim n\).

2.4.1 LEND (Linear Encoder, Non-Linear Decoder)
LEND resolves this asymmetry by keeping the encoder strictly linear on the Stiefel/NSA-Flow manifold while parameterizing the decoder as a multi-layer perceptron (Figure 2.4): \[
\text{Encoder (OLEE): } \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \qquad \text{Decoder: } \hat{\mathbf{X}}_m = \text{MLP}_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{Z}_m)
\] Because \(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\), LEND retains exact first-layer attribution and closed-form counterfactuals at test time while allowing \(\text{MLP}_{\theta_m}\) to absorb non-linear observational curvature during training.

text:
2.5 Stage 5: Bijective Normalizing Flows Downstream of OLEE (Flow-SiMR-V vs. Flow-SiMR)
Although LEND provides non-linear decoding, an MLP decoder \(g_{\theta_m}: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\) is not analytically invertible and does not endow the latent space with an exact probability density for closed-form conditional inference across missing views or geodesic path integration.

2.5.1 Full-Space Flow-SiMR vs. OLEE-Projected Flow-SiMR-V
We distinguish two normalizing flow architectures in src/pysimlr/flows.py:

Full-Space Normalizing Flow (Flow-SiMR, Figure 2.7): Applies an invertible sequence of RealNVP affine coupling layers directly on the ambient feature space \(\mathbb{R}^{p_m} \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\): \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = \text{Flow}_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{X}_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}
\tag{2.41}\] partitioning the output into shared coordinates \(\mathbf{Z}_{m, 1:k}\) and private coordinates \(\mathbf{Z}_{m, k+1:p_m}\). While exact on low-dimensional views, Flow-SiMR scales as \(\mathcal{O}(p_m^2)\) per coupling layer and sacrifices input linearity.
OLEE-Projected Latent Normalizing Flow (Flow-SiMR-V, Figure 2.8): Projects each modality onto the \(k\)-dimensional Stiefel/NSA-Flow manifold first, then applies an invertible RealNVP + ActNorm flow strictly within \(\mathbb{R}^k\): \[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}, \quad \mathbf{Z}_m = \text{Flow}_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}
\tag{2.42}\]

2.5.2 Proposition: Rectangular OLEE Prior Collapse and the Detached-Prior Solution
Combining a rectangular Stiefel projection \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\) (\(p_m > k\)) with a normalizing flow introduces a subtle variational pathology if the Gaussian prior negative log-likelihood (NLL) is backpropagated naively into \(\mathbf{V}_m\).
Proposition (Rectangular OLEE Variance Collapse under Unconstrained Flow Prior Gradients):
Let \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) with \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\) (\(p_m > k\)), and let \(\mathbf{Z}_m = f_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}})\) be a diffeomorphism on \(\mathbb{R}^k\) regularized by the standard normal prior negative log-likelihood: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}(\mathbf{V}_m, \psi_m) = \frac{1}{2n} \left\| f_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m) \right\|_F^2 - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log \left| \det J_{f_{\psi_m}}\left(\mathbf{x}_{m, i} \mathbf{V}_m\right) \right|
\] While the square bijection \(f_{\psi_m}: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k\) is prevented from trivially contracting its output by its own log-Jacobian barrier \(-\log |\det J_{f_{\psi_m}}|\), the rectangular projection \(\mathbf{V}_m: \mathbb{R}^{p_m} \to \mathbb{R}^k\) has no log-determinant term in \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}\). Consequently, for any fixed flow with bounded Lipschitz constant, minimizing \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}\) with respect to \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\) drives \(\mathbf{V}_m\) toward the minimum-variance eigenvectors of the sample covariance \(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{X}_m\): \[
\arg\min_{\mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m)} \frac{1}{2n} \|\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\|_F^2 = \text{span}\{ \mathbf{e}_{p_m - k + 1}, \dots, \mathbf{e}_{p_m} \}
\] rotating \(\mathbf{V}_m\) out of the biological signal subspace and into the lowest-variance noise directions (empirically collapsing \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{X}_1 \mathbf{V}_1)\) on ADNI-MCI from \(29.53\) at initialization to \(1.79\)).
Solution (Detached-Prior Variational Objective with ActNorm Scale Preservation):
In FlowSiMRVModel.forward (src/pysimlr/flows.py:920-934), we evaluate the normalizing flow prior NLL on the stop-gradient (detached) first-layer coordinates \(\text{sg}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}})\) while keeping the full computational graph active for cross-view alignment and feature reconstruction: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow-SiMR-V}}(\mathbf{V}_m, \psi_m) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}\left(\mathbf{X}_m, f_{\psi_m}^{-1}(\mathbf{U}_m) \mathbf{V}_m^\top\right) + \lambda_{\text{sim}} w_m \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\left(f_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m), \mathbf{U}_m\right) + \beta_{\text{prior}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}\left(f_{\psi_m}(\text{sg}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m))\right) + \gamma D(\mathbf{V}_m)
\tag{2.43}\] In this factored objective: 1. The first-layer basis \(\mathbf{V}_m\) is updated strictly by cross-view alignment \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\), ambient reconstruction \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}\), and Stiefel regularization \(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\)—never by the variance-shrinking prior norm. 2. The first layer of \(f_{\psi_m}\) is an invertible ActNorm layer initialized to \(s = -\log \text{std}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m^{(0)})\), which maps \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\) to unit scale in the forward pass and automatically restores the true physical scale of \(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) during the inverse pass \(f_{\psi_m}^{-1}(\mathbf{U}_m) \mathbf{V}_m^\top\).


2.5.3 Invertible Affine Coupling, Schur-Complement Conditional Inference, and Geodesics
Each flow \(f_{\psi_m}\) is a composition of RealNVP affine coupling layers (Dinh et al. 2016; Rezende and Mohamed 2015) with binary mask \(\mathbf{b} \in \{0, 1\}^k\): \[
\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{b} \odot \mathbf{z}, \quad \mathbf{z}_2 = (1 - \mathbf{b}) \odot \left( \mathbf{z} \odot e^{s(\mathbf{z}_1)} + t(\mathbf{z}_1) \right), \quad \mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{z}_2
\tag{2.44}\] with exact analytical inverse: \[
\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{b} \odot \mathbf{z}', \quad \mathbf{z}_2 = (1 - \mathbf{b}) \odot \left( (\mathbf{z}' - t(\mathbf{z}_1)) \odot e^{-s(\mathbf{z}_1)} \right), \quad \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{z}_2
\tag{2.45}\] Modeling the concatenated shared latent coordinates across views as a joint Gaussian: \[
\mathbf{Z}_{\text{joint}} = [\mathbf{Z}_{1,\text{shared}} \parallel \dots \parallel \mathbf{Z}_{M,\text{shared}}] \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)
\tag{2.46}\] yields closed-form conditional cross-view inference for an unobserved view \(B\) given observed view(s) \(A\) via the Schur complement: \[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B|A} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_B + \Sigma_{BA} \Sigma_{AA}^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_{A,\text{shared}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_A), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{X}}_B = f_{\psi_B}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B|A}) \mathbf{V}_B^\top
\tag{2.47}\]

3.1.1 Multi-Modal Data Regimes, Data Hygiene, and Replication Structure
To evaluate multi-modal architectures across distinct inductive biases and biomedical domains, we establish a unified benchmark protocol mirroring the five deductive stages of Chapter 2 across 12 multi-modal data regimes: 6 controlled synthetic manifolds with known ground-truth latents \(\mathbf{U}^*\) and bases \(\mathbf{V}^*\), plus 6 established real-world clinical, multi-omics, and neuroimaging cohorts evaluated across \(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\) independent random seeds (\([42, 43, 44]\)) and 9 model architectures (\(12 \times 3 \times 9 = 324\) total model evaluations, with private_scale = 0.5, consolidate = False, and iteration-0 linear warm-start initialization), complemented by a 1,214-combination hyperparameter sweep and a 10-seed mediation benchmark on ADNI-MCI (\(N = 1,084\)).
Following Demšar (2006), global statistical inference is conducted on the \(B = 12\) independent dataset blocks (build_ranking_blocks in src/pysimlr/benchmarks/deep_ranking.py), averaging replicates within each \((\text{Dataset}, \text{Model})\) cell before ranking so repeated seeds never inflate degrees of freedom. Across all real-world cohorts, we enforce three strict data-hygiene invariants:

In-Fold Standardization & Covariate Adjustment: Feature standardization (StandardScaler) and Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) demographic covariate residualization (AGE, PTGENDER, PTEDUCAT on ADNI-MCI) are fitted exclusively on the training partition and applied to the test partition without leakage.
Column Completeness Filtering (\(\ge 98\%\)): High-missingness features (\(\ge 2\%\) missing values, such as sparse clinical scales MOCA and Ecog on ADNI-MCI or incomplete assay probes in TCGA) are excluded prior to median imputation so degenerate constant-imputed columns cannot distort cross-view covariance.
Partial-View Out-of-Sample Evaluation (eval_view_indices): When a clinical target view is used during bipartite training (ADNI-MCI View 4), that view is strictly withheld at test time (eval_view_indices = [0, 1, 2]), and single-matrix baselines (PCA, NSAFlow-PCA) are fitted exclusively on the predictor views ([0, 1, 2]).



3.1.2 Established Real-World Biomedical and Multi-View Cohorts

Cleveland Heart Disease (Heart, \(N=297\), 2 views: \(p_1=7, p_2=6\)):

Cohort Source & Filtering: Drawn from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (processed.cleveland.data, cached locally at data/heart_cleveland.csv) (Detrano et al. 1989). Six records with missing entries (?) are removed, yielding \(N=297\) complete patients.
View Partitioning: \(V_1\) (\(p_1=7\): resting vitals and history age, sex, cp, trestbps, chol, fbs, restecg) and \(V_2\) (\(p_2=6\): stress electrocardiography and fluoroscopy thalach, exang, oldpeak, slope, ca, thal).
Downstream Task & Results: Binary coronary artery disease diagnosis (num > 0, majority rate \(53.9\%\)). In the 3-seed benchmark, NSAFlow-PCA achieves the highest strictly linear probe accuracy (\(84.8\%\)), while NSAFlow-PCA and PCA achieve \(83.7\%\) consensus accuracy and SiMLR-LBFGSB / SiMLR-LBFGS reach \(83.7\%\) on the linear OLEE probe.

Diabetes Progression (Diabetes, \(N=442\), 2 views: \(p_1=5, p_2=5\)):

Cohort Source: The Efron et al. clinical diabetes cohort (Efron et al. 2004) (sklearn.datasets.load_diabetes).
View Partitioning: \(V_1\) (\(p_1=5\): age, sex, bmi, bp, total serum cholesterol s1) and \(V_2\) (\(p_2=5\): specialized blood serum panel s2–s6).
Downstream Task & Results: Continuous 1-year disease progression (\(R^2\)). NSAFlow-PCA leads global consensus prediction (\(R^2 = 0.382\)), while SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(R^2 = 0.396\)) and SiMLR-LBFGS (\(R^2 = 0.396\)) lead the strictly linear OLEE probe (vs. PCA \(0.351\)).

TCGA-BRCA 3-View Multi-Omics (MultiOmics, \(N=822\), 3 views: \(p=[200, 150, 150]\)):

Cohort Source: The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma cohort (data/tcga/brca_er_cached.npz, filtered at \(\ge 98\%\) completeness) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016).
View Partitioning: \(V_1\) (\(p_1=200\): top-variance mRNA HiSeqV2 transcripts), \(V_2\) (\(p_2=150\): somatic GISTIC2 CNV), and \(V_3\) (\(p_3=150\): RPPA targeted proteomics).
Downstream Task & Results: Binary classification of Estrogen Receptor (ER) status (ER+ prevalence \(76.4\%\)). NSAFlow-PCA leads global consensus accuracy (\(92.7\%\)), while SiMLR-LBFGS, SiMLR-LBFGSB, LEND, and Flow-SiMR-V achieve \(92.6\%\) on the strictly linear OLEE probe.

TCGA-KIRC 3-View Renal Oncology (TCGA-KIRC, \(N=467\), 3 views: \(p=[200, 150, 150]\)):

Cohort Source: The Cancer Genome Atlas Kidney Renal Clear Cell Carcinoma cohort (data/tcga/kirc_stage_cached.npz, filtered at \(\ge 98\%\) completeness) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013).
View Partitioning: Three co-registered molecular views across \(N=467\) primary tumors: mRNA expression (\(p_1=200\)), GISTIC2 copy-number variation (\(p_2=150\)), and RPPA proteomics (\(p_3=150\)).
Downstream Task & Results: Binary classification of pathologic tumor stage (late stage III/IV vs. early stage I/II). Flow-SiMR-V and LEND lead global consensus accuracy (\(69.7\%\)), while SiMLR, SiMLR-LBFGS, and SiMLR-LBFGSB achieve \(68.6\%\) on the linear OLEE probe.

ADNI-MCI 4-View Neurodegeneration Cohort (ADNI-MCI, \(N=1,084\), 4 views: \(p=[160, 160, 62, 11]\)):

Cohort Source: \(N=1,084\) participants with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008).
View Partitioning: Three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) features: DKT gray-matter volumes \(p_1=160\), hierarchical cortical thickness \(p_2=160\), native T1w thickness \(p_3=62\)) and a fourth view containing the 11 \(>98\%\)-complete clinical/cognitive scores (ADAS11, ADAS13, ADASQ4, MMSE, CDRSB, TRABSCOR, FAQ, and 4 RAVLT sub-scores), with in-fold FWL adjustment for AGE, PTGENDER, and PTEDUCAT.
Downstream Task & Results: Under Protocol B (bipartite training graph {0:[3], 1:[3], 2:[3], 3:[0,1,2]}, View 4 withheld at test time), models predict the primary multi-domain cognitive axis (CogPC1 R^2) from the 3 MRI views alone. Across 3 seeds in the global benchmark, SiMLR-LBFGSB achieves CogPC1 R^2 \(= \mathbf{0.2237}\) on the strictly linear OLEE probe (and \(0.1830\) on the 3-dimension consensus \(\mathbf{U}\)), outperforming single-matrix PCA (\(0.1522\)) by \(+47\%\). In our 1,214-combination sweep (Section 3.4), SiMLR-Lookahead reaches \(0.2407\), NEDPP reaches \(0.2357\), and Flow-SiMR-V reaches \(0.2341\). In our 10-seed mediation benchmark, modeling the two-step pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Cognition} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)) boosts daily disability prediction over 6-fold (LEND-SiMR + MAI: \(R^2 = 0.2648\) vs. direct MRI \(0.0411\)).

UCI Multiple Features Handwritten Digits (mfeat, \(N=2,000\), 4 views: \(p=[76, 64, 6, 47]\)):

Cohort Source: Four geometric and spectral descriptor views (Fourier coefficients \(p_1=76\), Karhunen–Loève projections \(p_2=64\), morphological features \(p_3=6\), Zernike moments \(p_4=47\)) across \(N=2,000\) handwritten digits (\(10\) balanced classes, \(k=3\)).
Downstream Task & Results: 10-class digit classification accuracy. Flow-SiMR-V leads 3-dimensional consensus accuracy (\(81.9\%\)) followed by LEND (\(78.9\%\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(77.1\%\)) vs. NSAFlow-PCA (\(70.7\%\)) and PCA (\(73.2\%\)). On the concatenated \(12\)-dimensional first-layer OLEE probe (\(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\)), cross-view Stiefel models reach \(94.4\%\text{–}96.2\%\) vs. \(72.7\%\) for PCA.

3.1.3 Controlled Synthetic Generative Regimes
To test distinct, non-overlapping hypotheses about multi-view recovery \((\mathbf{U}^*, \mathbf{V}^*)\) under private_scale = 0.5, synthetic_cases.py defines six synthetic generative regimes:

Clean Linear Multi-View Manifold (Linear, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[100, 80, 60]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \mathbf{U}^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where shared latent scales \([1.2, 1.0, 0.85]\) exceed view-private background (\(\sigma_{\text{priv}} = 0.5\)) and Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 0.5\)). Tests baseline recovery where linear and cross-view OLEE models perform at parity (\(R^2 = 0.972\text{–}0.990\), whereas unconstrained NED drops to \(0.713\)).
Polynomial Latent Warping (Polynomial, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[120, 80, 50]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \psi_m^{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{U}^*) \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where \(\psi_m^{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{U}^*)\) applies non-cancelling quadratic, cross-product, and cubic distortions in \(\mathbb{R}^k\) prior to linear projection \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top\). Flow-SiMR-V leads global consensus prediction (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.925}\) vs. \(0.870\) for PCA), while linear probes on \(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) reach \(0.903\text{–}0.916\).
Sinusoidal Periodic Warping (Sine, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[120, 80, 50]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \psi_m^{\text{sin}}(\mathbf{U}^*) \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where \(\psi_m^{\text{sin}}(\mathbf{U}^*)\) combines linear coordinates with trigonometric oscillations (\(\sin\) and \(\cos\) couplings), with SiMLR-LBFGS (\(0.935\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(0.934\)) leading consensus recovery.
Asymmetric Shared-Plus-Private Manifold (Shared+Private, \(N=1,000, K_{\text{sh}}=3, K_{\text{pr}}=2, p=[160, 60, 30]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \mathbf{U}_{\text{shared}}^* \mathbf{V}_{m, \text{sh}}^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m, \text{pr}}^* \mathbf{V}_{m, \text{pr}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where shared scales decay (\([1.0, 0.625, 0.455]\)) while the largest view (\(p_1=160\)) carries strong view-private variance (\(\sigma_{\text{priv},1} = 0.80\)). Single-matrix concatenation (PCA \(R^2 = 0.639\), NSAFlow-PCA \(R^2 = 0.629\)) is pulled toward View 1’s private variance, whereas cross-view consensus in LEND (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.949}\), \(CMC = 0.896\)) and Flow-SiMR-V (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.845}\), linear probe \(0.908\)) isolates the shared manifold.
Non-Negative Disjoint Parts — Dominant Signal (NonnegParts, \(N=400, K=3, p=[120, 45, 30]\)): Ground-truth loading matrices \(\mathbf{V}_m^* \ge \mathbf{0}\) have strictly disjoint column supports across the \(K=3\) components, and the outcome tracks the dominant shared component (\(u_1^*\)). Bound-constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB recovers the true sparse support with Jaccard/F1 score \(0.991\) (followed by SiMLR-LBFGS at \(0.966\), LEND at \(0.899\), and Flow-SiMR-V at \(0.826\)), whereas unconstrained PCA scores at the random-partition chance floor (\(0.333\)).
Non-Negative Disjoint Parts — Weak Signal (NonnegPartsWeak, \(N=400, K=3, p=[120, 45, 30]\)): Identical disjoint non-negative basis \(\mathbf{V}_m^*\), but the outcome is driven by the weakest shared component (\(u_3^*\)). Because single-matrix concatenation absorbs view-private noise into its leading components, PCA drops to \(R^2 = 0.522\) and NSAFlow-PCA to \(0.570\), whereas LEND (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.732}\)), SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.716}\)), SiMLR-LBFGS (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.716}\)), and Flow-SiMR-V (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.703}\)) isolate the weak shared component via cross-view alignment and non-negativity.

3.2.1 Multi-Objective 4-Axis Pareto Frontier Analysis
Models are evaluated across four complementary operational axes (Figure 3.3):

3.3 Testing Stage 1: The Input Boundary — OLEE Geometry, Support Recovery & Attribution Audits
Stage 1 of our deductive formulation predicts that restricting the input boundary to a Stiefel projection \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) regularized by nsa_flow achieves three simultaneous properties: (1) near-zero per-view frame defect \(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) and exact zero signed lobe crosstalk (\(\|\mathbf{V}_m^+ \odot \mathbf{V}_m^-\|_1 = 0\)), (2) accurate recovery of disjoint sparse feature supports (Support_Recovery_V) where dense SVD/PCA is rotationally blind, and (3) exact individual-patient feature attribution without post-hoc surrogate error.

3.3.1 Sparse Disjoint Support Recovery & Subspace Identifiability








Figure 3.4: Ground-Truth Latent Coordinate Recovery (Canonical Mean Correlation on \(\mathbf{U}\)) across the 6 Synthetic Generative Regimes. LEND leads overall (\(CMC = 0.907\)), especially on Shared+Private (\(0.896\) vs \(0.636\) for PCA) and NonnegParts (\(0.865\) vs \(0.740\) for PCA), while Flow-SiMR-V achieves \(CMC = 0.876\) overall and \(0.880\) on Shared+Private.





As shown in Table 3.2 and Figure 3.4:

Exact Disjoint Support Recovery on NonnegParts & NonnegPartsWeak: Because PCA is invariant to orthogonal rotations inside \(\text{span}(\mathbf{V})\), its dense mixed-sign basis scores at the random-partition chance floor (\(\text{Support } F_1 = \mathbf{0.333}\)). In contrast, bound-constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB recovers the true disjoint non-negative support with \(\text{Support } F_1 = \mathbf{0.991}\) (and SiMLR-LBFGS with \(\mathbf{0.966}\), LEND with \(\mathbf{0.899}\), and Flow-SiMR-V with \(\mathbf{0.826}\)). On NonnegPartsWeak (where the target depends on the weakest shared factor \(u_3^*\)), LEND (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.732}\)), SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.716}\)), SiMLR-LBFGS (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.716}\)), and Flow-SiMR-V (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.703}\)) outperform PCA (\(R^2 = 0.522\)) by nearly \(+20\) percentage points.

3.3.2 Clinical Attribution Audits: Direct Linear Derivatives vs. Post-Hoc Surrogates
Because the OLEE input mapping is an isometry (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m\)), individual-patient attributions \(\mathbf{c}_{m,ik} = \mathbf{x}_{m,i} \odot \mathbf{v}_{m,k}\) are exact and require zero perturbation sampling.

3.4 Testing Stage 2: Cross-View Consensus, Bipartite Topologies & ADNI-MCI Mediation
Stage 2 of our deductive formulation establishes that cross-view consensus topology (star, loo, and directed/bipartite graph) and scale-profiled alignment energies govern whether multi-view models isolate shared biological signal from view-private variance and background anatomy.

3.4.1 Cross-View Noise Rejection (Shared+Private) and LOO vs. Star Regularization

Asymmetric View-Private Noise (Shared+Private): When View 0 (\(p_1=160\)) carries heightened private variance (\(\sigma_{\text{priv},1} = 0.80\)), single-matrix concatenation (PCA \(R^2 = 0.639, CMC = 0.636\); NSAFlow-PCA \(R^2 = 0.629, CMC = 0.636\)) rotates its leading components toward View 0’s private subspace. By contrast, cross-view consensus in LEND (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.949}, CMC = \mathbf{0.896}\)) and Flow-SiMR-V (\(R^2 = \mathbf{0.845}, CMC = \mathbf{0.880}\), linear probe \(0.908\)) rejects View 0’s private noise and recovers all three shared factors.
Leave-One-Out (LOO) vs. Star Topology: In Star topology, modality \(m\) aligns to a consensus \(\mathbf{U}\) that includes its own projection \(\mathbf{Z}_m\). In LOO topology, modality \(m\) aligns exclusively against \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\), narrowing the train-test generalization gap on clinical cohorts (Figure 3.8 and Figure 3.9).

3.5 Testing Stage 3: Linear Multi-View Manifold Solvers & Complexity Scaling
Stage 3 of our deductive progression compares first-order Riemannian gradient descent (SiMLR) against quasi-Newton (SiMLR-LBFGS) and bound-constrained quasi-Newton (SiMLR-LBFGSB) solvers on \(\prod_m \text{St}(k, p_m)\):

Superior Real-Cohort Linear Basis Recovery (SiMLR-LBFGSB #1 Rank \(2.50\), SiMLR-LBFGS #2 Rank \(3.33\)): Across the 6 real-world biomedical cohorts (Heart, Diabetes, MultiOmics, TCGA-KIRC, ADNI-MCI, mfeat), SiMLR-LBFGSB and SiMLR-LBFGS rank #1 and #2 on the strictly linear OLEE probe (\(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\) mean \(0.670\) and \(0.663\) vs. \(0.612\) for PCA), and achieve \(0.991\) and \(0.966\) sparse support recovery on the non-negative synthetic regimes.
Complexity Scaling (\(\mathcal{O}(N)\) in Sample Size, \(\mathcal{O}(K^3)\) in Rank): Figure 3.10 confirms that execution wall-time scales linearly with sample size \(N\) (\(\mathcal{O}(N)\)) and cubically with latent rank \(K\) (\(\mathcal{O}(K^3)\) for the \(k \times k\) Gram and Sylvester/Newton-Schulz operations), remaining highly efficient across typical biomedical ranks (\(K \le 64\)).









Figure 3.10: Algorithmic Efficiency and Wall-Time Scaling. (Left) Sample size \(N\) scaling is strictly linear (\(\mathcal{O}(N)\)). (Right) Latent dimension \(K\) scaling reflects the \(k \times k\) Newton-Schulz and Gram matrix overhead (\(\mathcal{O}(K^3)\)).

section: 3.6 Testing Stage 4: Non-Linear Decoding Downstream of OLEE (LEND vs. NED & NEDPP)

3.6 Testing Stage 4: Non-Linear Decoding Downstream of OLEE (LEND vs. NED & NEDPP)
Stage 4 of our deductive formulation predicts that keeping the encoder strictly linear (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)) while placing non-linear MLP capacity in the decoder (LEND) captures curved generative manifolds without suffering the high-dimensional encoder overfitting that afflicts unconstrained deep encoders (NED, NEDPP):

Why LEND Ranks #1 on Global Consensus (\(3.58\)) and Synthetic OLEE Basis (\(2.50\)): Across the 12-dataset benchmark, LEND achieves the highest mean consensus score (\(0.760 \pm 0.249\)), the highest ground-truth latent recovery (\(CMC = \mathbf{0.907}\)), and the #1 synthetic rank (\(2.50\) on XV), outperforming NED by \(+0.1669\) (\(p_{\text{Holm}} = 2.7 \times 10^{-5}\)) and NEDPP by \(+0.1710\) (\(p_{\text{Holm}} = 2.7 \times 10^{-5}\)).
Why NED and NEDPP Collapse on Shared+Private and NonnegPartsWeak: When encoder MLPs \(f_{\text{enc},m}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m)\) are inserted before consensus formation, they warp view-private noise to artificially match the consensus target during training, causing test-set consensus \(R^2\) to collapse to \(0.429\) (NED) and \(0.523\) (NEDPP) on Shared+Private (vs. \(0.949\) for LEND), and to \(0.292\) (NED) and \(0.222\) (NEDPP) on NonnegPartsWeak (vs. \(0.732\) for LEND).
